draftPackage.topic: The dice with no best choice
draftPackage.centralQuestion: How can each of four dice have another die that is more likely to beat it?
draftPackage.thesis: Fair face selection can yield a circular chain of pairwise probability advantages; a strongest die need not exist.
draftPackage.viewerPayoff: Reconstruct why the specified dice form a2/3 counter-choice circle without confusing probability with guaranteed wins.

sources.title: Non-transitive Dice
sources.notes: Institutional mathematical demonstration with explicit face labels and conditional game; primary source for its own example. No physical experiment. Its prose introducing mixed-case formulas says multiplying probabilities; we independently sum the disjoint cases. Formula images not inspected.

sources.title: Nontransitive and Balanced Sets of Dice
sources.notes: Mathematics department seminar abstract corroborates the four-way2/3 cycle; no explicit face assignments/full proof. Different letter conventions are presentation labels.

sources.title: Efron’s Dice
sources.notes: Mathematical reference corroborates balanced four-die cyclic odds and distinguishes a separate set with ties. Diagram face values not inspected and not used as source for exact configuration.

sources.organization: Levi Angel and Matt Davis, Muskingum University
sources.title: A Direct Construction of Non-Transitive Dice Sets
sources.notes: Author research preprint; introduction defines dominance by P(X>Y)>1/2 and gives a separate three-sided5/9 example. Supports the mathematical distinction and open class, not the selected four-die face values. Only introductory extracted PDF text inspected; no screenshot/full-proof review or peer-reviewed status claimed.

draftAsset.editorialPurpose: Reconstruct why the specified dice form a2/3 counter-choice circle without confusing probability with guaranteed wins.
draftAsset.storyAngle: A mentally participatory choice becomes a visible proof that matchup odds need not rank dice linearly.

segments.text: You choose first. I choose second—and I can get better odds, whichever die you pick. Higher number wins.
These dice have unusual numbers. For this puzzle, each face is equally likely, and one roll doesn’t affect the other.
Yellow always rolls three. Orange has four twos and two sixes. Yellow beats four of those six faces: a two-thirds chance.
But blue has four fours and two zeros. It beats yellow with every four—also two-thirds.
Switch to blue? Green has three fives and three ones. Its fives beat every blue face. Even its ones beat blue’s zeros. That adds up to twenty-four winning combinations out of thirty-six.
Then orange has better odds against green: its sixes beat every face, and its twos beat green’s ones. Again, twenty-four out of thirty-six.
The advantages form a circle. Every die has a counter with a two-thirds chance.
You can still win—or lose—any roll. Choosing second gives an informed player the advantage.
There’s no best die in this set. The better choice depends on what it’s up against.

narrativeStructure.label: choice
narrativeStructure.purpose: The viewer makes a mental choice and knows the high-number rule before decoding probabilities. Four inspectable large dice presented as a challenge, no dominant lecture title.

narrativeStructure.label: conditions
narrativeStructure.purpose: Clarify unusual values and mathematical conditions. Reveal each die’s repeated-face signature through local turns; no fair-physical-dice certification.

narrativeStructure.label: first-proof
narrativeStructure.purpose: Build the simplest proof. Keep a single yellow3 as the reference; unfold orange’s six equally likely faces into a shallow semicircle, highlight the four2s that lose and retain the two6s that win.

narrativeStructure.label: reconsider
narrativeStructure.purpose: Let the viewer reconsider. Blue enters as the response to yellow; its four4s and two0s split visibly. Different opposition changes the answer without a new full table.

narrativeStructure.label: green-reply
narrativeStructure.purpose: Green looks weak with ones, then reveals two disjoint winning routes. Use a half-and-half green split: all18 pairs in the5 branch win; in the1 branch, six pairs against blue0s win and twelve against4s lose. Build24/36 from18+6; blocks sized to multiplicity, not four equally weighted value types.

narrativeStructure.label: orange-return
narrativeStructure.purpose: Orange returns as a plausible surprise with two6s. Twelve pairs for6 beat every green face; twelve pairs for2 against green1 win; twelve2-versus5 pairs lose. Build24/36 as12+12, using the established visual grammar but a purposeful re-fold/re-pairing, not replaying another grid.

narrativeStructure.label: closure
narrativeStructure.purpose: Keep orange visible as yellow re-enters; the apparently best counter is itself countered. Start closing accumulated matchup marks.

narrativeStructure.label: circle
narrativeStructure.purpose: Pull back to all four physical identities with a closed counter-choice loop. Arrow direction explicitly means more likely to beat; show the original first choice still has a response.

narrativeStructure.label: chance
narrativeStructure.purpose: Show one losing possible outcome briefly while the2/3 label remains; label it possible outcome, not random experimental result. Put the informed second-choice decision in context.

narrativeStructure.label: payoff
narrativeStructure.purpose: Settle on the closed loop, then emphasize one die beside two different opponents. Same object, different matchup: the exact opening promise is answered without an engagement outro.
